extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decisionmakers, and institutional legal/compliance staff
extracted.subtask_description: Federal regulatory guidance on designing and implementing grievance procedures for sex-based harassment at postsecondary institutions, including rules on disclosure, privacy, live questioning/hearings, evidentiary access, and due-process protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on disclosures of information obtained solely through grievance procedures (§106.46(e)(6)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must limit disclosures of information and evidence obtained solely through the sex-based harassment grievance procedures; §106.46(e)(6)(iii) is narrowly framed to address privacy concerns related to such information and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures of such information should generally be restricted; institutions may authorize narrow disclosures to particular individuals or of particular pieces of evidence depending on circumstances. The provision is limited to information obtained solely through the grievance procedures and does not restrict disclosures based on information learned through other means (e.g., personal experience) or restrict journalists. Institutions must implement measures to prevent unauthorized disclosure and inform parties/advisors about permissible/ prohibited disclosures. The Department added that disclosures for administrative proceedings or litigation related to the complaint are authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized disclosures include those permitted under §106.45(b)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorized disclosures for purposes of §106.46(e)(6)(iii) include those disclosures that are permitted under §106.45(b)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(b)(5) prohibits taking steps to protect privacy that restrict parties' ability to gather evidence, consult family/confidential resources/advisors, or otherwise prepare for or participate in grievance procedures. Thus institutions must balance privacy protections with parties' rights to gather evidence and consult support people or advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must inform parties/advisors about permissible and prohibited disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent unauthorized disclosure, institutions must ensure that parties and their advisors are aware of any types of disclosures that are permissible (including those authorized by the institution, other laws, or party consent) and which disclosures are prohibited by the institution or other laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exercising discretion to authorize certain disclosures, the institution must still satisfy its §106.45(b)(5) obligation to take reasonable steps to protect privacy. Reasonable steps may include policies that protect sensitive evidence and software that restricts further distribution of evidence beyond those who need access in the grievance procedure. Institutions should communicate clearly the limits on redistribution and use (for example, limitations on physical copies or redisclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable steps to protect privacy under §106.45(b)(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must take reasonable steps to protect the parties' and witnesses' privacy during the pendency of grievance procedures, while not restricting their ability to participate or gather evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable steps may include administrative policies, technological controls (e.g., software restricting distribution), and procedural limits on copying/redistribution. Widespread authorization to disclose information obtained solely through grievance procedures could violate §106.45(b)(5) by failing to take reasonable steps to protect privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must prevent and address unauthorized disclosures but are not required to impose penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.46(e)(6)(iii) requires institutions to prevent and address unauthorized disclosures by parties and their advisors; addressing such disclosures may include penalizing unauthorized disclosures, but the Department declines to require mandatory penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should take into account the specific circumstances of the unauthorized disclosure when determining how to respond. The regulation expects institutions to implement this provision consistent with the First Amendment and §106.6(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA interaction and overrides for disclosure of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When Title IX regulations require disclosure of evidence that would not comply with FERPA, the GEPA override (and in some circumstances constitutional override) applies and requires disclosure of evidence under §106.46(e)(6) to parties and their advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FERPA defines 'education records' and generally limits disclosure, but GEPA and constitutional overrides permit disclosure to parties/advisors when Title IX requires it. An eligible student can consent to disclosure of their own records, but where records are not directly related to a student, GEPA override may permit sharing with advisors of choice. Institutions must still take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorized redisclosure and may limit physical copies or use restrictions despite FERPA not limiting a student's use/redisclosure of their own education records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity to access relevant evidence or investigative report (§106.46(e)(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: A postsecondary institution must provide the parties and their advisors with an equal opportunity to access the evidence that is relevant to the allegations of sex-based harassment and not otherwise impermissible; if providing an investigative report, provide equal access to either the relevant evidence or the same written investigative report that accurately summarizes the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement applies to parties and advisors equally rather than leaving the decision to the party to share with an advisor. Upon a request for an investigative report, the institution must provide equal opportunity to access the underlying relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-questioning process requirement when credibility is in dispute (§106.46(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: All postsecondary institutions must provide a live-questioning process that enables the decisionmaker to assess the credibility of parties and witnesses if credibility is in dispute and relevant to evaluating one or more allegations of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The live-questioning process must be provided either through (1) individual meetings with the investigator or decisionmaker, who will ask initial and follow-up questions proposed by the parties as well as their own questions, or (2) a live hearing with questions (including questions proposed by the parties) asked by the decisionmaker or the party's advisor. Each party must have an opportunity to have their relevant and not otherwise impermissible questions asked. The investigator or decisionmaker must consider all relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence. Institutions are given flexibility to choose the format based on their administrative structure, resources, and applicable law while ensuring meaningful opportunity to be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conflicts of interest and bias for Title IX personnel (§106.45(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinator, investigators, and decisionmakers are prohibited from having a conflict of interest or bias for or against complainants or respondents generally or an individual complainant or respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must ensure impartiality in personnel administering grievance procedures. Final §106.8(d)(2) requires training for investigators, decisionmakers, and others responsible for implementing grievance procedures on how to serve impartially, including avoiding prejudgment, conflicts of interest, and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that respondent is not responsible until determination (§106.45(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures require a presumption that the respondent is not responsible for the alleged sex discrimination until a determination is made at the conclusion of the recipient's grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is part of procedural protections to ensure fairness and is coupled with objective evaluation of evidence and other equitable-treatment requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evaluation of all relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence (§106.45(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must require an objective evaluation of all evidence that is relevant and not otherwise impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators and decisionmakers must consider all such evidence when assessing allegations. This requirement supports reliable outcomes and equitable treatment of parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment of parties and appeal rights (§106.45(b)(1); §106.46(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must carry out grievance procedures in a nondiscriminatory manner and treat the parties equitably; the regulations also provide for appeal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable treatment includes ensuring equal opportunities, nondiscrimination based on sex, and procedural protections such as notice, opportunity to be heard, and access to appeals consistent with the regulatory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process framing — notice and meaningful opportunity to be heard
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations are intended to satisfy fundamental due process rights of notice and opportunity to be heard, while balancing parties' interests and institutional interests; what constitutes a meaningful opportunity may depend on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considered Mathews-type balancing (private interest, risk of erroneous deprivation/benefit of additional procedures, government interest including burden/cost). The regulations allow flexibility (live questioning options) tailored to achieve reliable outcomes, protect parties, and minimize chilling effects on reporting while considering institutional burdens.
